children: By Staff Writer
South Africa's aviation regulator says it is investigating Airlink's low-level fly-past over Cape Town Stadium after the spectacle drew concern at home and abroad.
The South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it had obtained flight data from the airline and requested additional information as part of its review of the 29 August display.
Airlink has since withdrawn its application for a third fly-past, which had been planned for the following weekend. SACAA did not give a reason for the decision.

Two Airlink Embraer 190 aircraft flew over the packed stadium before the Springboks' 33-26 victory over New Zealand. One was painted in Springbok colours and the other in an All Blacks-inspired livery.

The fly-past was intended to celebrate the rugby rivalry, but footage appearing to show the aircraft passing close to the stadium roof spread rapidly online and raised questions about the manoeuvre's safety.

SACAA said Airlink had applied for permission to conduct three overflights linked to the rugby matches. The first took place in Johannesburg on 22 August, followed by the Cape Town display a week later. Both were approved.

For the Cape Town operation, the airline submitted supporting documents and carried out a simulator practice flight and a safety briefing. SACAA said these preparations were conducted in line with regulations governing special air events.

The regulator nevertheless began further checks after the public debate."Following various discussions in the media relating to the events of the past weekend, the SACAA initiated compliance verifications, engaged the operator, obtained the Flight Data Recording downloads, as well as other additional requirements," it said.

SACAA said it was analysing the information and would issue a report with recommendations once the assessment was complete. The review is expected to establish whether the aircraft remained within the approved altitude and complied with all conditions set by the regulator.

A Johannesburg-based commercial airline pilot, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of corporate media policies, said footage taken from the ground could not, on its own, establish whether the aircraft flew below the approved height."If they were cleared to be at 200 feet and then they executed at 200 feet, then that's that," the pilot said.
Flight recorders would provide the most reliable account of the aircraft's altitude, speed and flight path, he added.

The pilot said such displays were not unusual but required careful preparation."Flyovers are nothing new. It's an incredible display which requires a lot of precision, a lot of planning, and when done correctly, it's just beautiful to see," he said.

He acknowledged, however, that flying two passenger aircraft at low altitude over a crowded stadium carried risks, particularly in Cape Town's unpredictable wind conditions."That's a very risky manoeuvre, I won't lie to you. Cape Town has some of the most terrible winds that you can ever experience anywhere in the world," he said.
Divided opinionSmoke from pyrotechnics, changing weather conditions and the handling of heavy aircraft were among the factors that needed to be considered, he added.
The fly-past evoked memories of the 1995 Rugby World Cup final, when a South African Airways Boeing 747 flew over Ellis Park shortly before the Springboks defeated the All Blacks.

But while the 1995 display became part of South African rugby folklore, the latest one has divided opinion. Many spectators celebrated it, while critics questioned whether such a manoeuvre should be conducted over a packed venue.

SACAA said aviation safety remained paramount and "not negotiable". It also defended South Africa's safety record, saying the country had recorded no fatal accidents in commercial airline operations for more than four decades.
The regulator said South Africa was ranked seventh in the world and first in Africa for aviation safety standards by the International Civil Aviation Organization.

The pilot said the concerns raised by the public should still be taken seriously, even if the review finds that Airlink complied with the terms of its approval."All the rules we have in aviation were written in blood. When you've got a 50,000- or 60,000-capacity stadium full and anything happens, all those lives are at risk," he said."Just because you can do something doesn't mean you always should."
